record.tranche_reason: The study applies sparse autoencoders and feature analyses to Claude 3 Sonnet, a large language model, and reports results about recovered features. This extends feature-based evidence to a new model setting; it does not reproduce the original toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition and treats superposition as part of its motivation, but does not test toy-model geometry, a sparsity-dependent transition, or the capacity account of polysemanticity. It reports SAE feature and neuron comparisons, feature splitting, and incomplete feature coverage; those results are recorded below. Steering examples are not evidence that the behavior arises without intervention.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on Claude 3 Sonnet's middle residual stream, a new large-model setting. It reports how sparse the recovered features are, how they correlate with neurons, and how interpretable they are, which bears on V4. It also reports incomplete concept coverage and dictionary-size-dependent splitting, which bears on V5. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. SAEs yield interpretable, abstract, causally influential features in Claude 3 Sonnet. The authors stress that the inventory is far from complete, that splitting and shrinkage issues remain, and that superposition is 'still isn't that tested'. They consider higher-dimensional feature manifolds plausible.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse autoencoders on a large language model's middle-layer residual-stream activations and evaluates recovered features; it does not reproduce the original toy-network setup or its geometric experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature resolution and coverage vary with SAE dictionary size: the San Francisco feature splits into more specific features in larger dictionaries, and larger SAEs find features for rarer concepts.
record.problems: The model size is undisclosed. The study analyzes only the middle residual-stream layer and acknowledges incomplete feature coverage, possible cross-layer superposition, and an imperfect loss proxy for interpretability. Some interpretability comparisons are reported only qualitatively, without effect sizes or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Steering examples and individual feature case studies are not included as rows for V4 because they involve deliberately clamped activations and do not measure naturally occurring prevalence or the completeness of feature recovery. The study's frequency-versus-feature-coverage analyses are also omitted because they do not directly measure the claim versions' stated geometry or canonicality.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity-dependent phase transition, or geometry analysis.
Capacity allocation (dedicated vs shared dimensions) is not tested.
No test of non-capacity origins of polysemantic neurons.
Stability across seeds or training procedures, and canonicality across layers, are not tested.
Only discussed: authors call higher-dimensional feature manifolds 'quite plausible'; no experiment.
Only one model and one layer (the middle residual stream) are studied.

missing.what: Concept coverage vs. training-data frequency: a concept becomes >50% likely to have a feature at a frequency slightly below 1/alive-features; the 34M SAE has only ~12M alive features. Bears on V5 completeness and dependence on dictionary size.
Dead-feature proportions: ~2% (1M), 35% (4M), 65% (34M), plus the 65% variance-explained bound. These bear on how complete the dictionary is.
Manual inspection of 50 neurons found them 'typically activating in multiple unrelated contexts' (polysemantic neurons in the LLM).

record.verdict_notes: The steering results are induced interventions and are correctly excluded. The frequency-coverage analysis was left out of the rows, but it bears on V5 completeness and should be added as a row.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transition, and regular geometry are not tested.
The capacity account of polysemanticity and the proposed allocation of dedicated versus shared dimensions are not tested.
The study does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise from mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
The study examines one proprietary model, a middle residual-stream layer, and the reported SAE runs; it does not establish that this pattern generalizes across models or layers.

It reports incomplete concept coverage and splitting across dictionary sizes, but does not test feature stability across random seeds, training procedures, or layers, nor establish that SAE features are canonical units.
The study does not experimentally compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional feature representations.
